approachQuestion.prompt:
Bundle reorderable letter codes

Input: an array words of strings using only the 26 lowercase English letters. Group original indices so that two indices share a group exactly when their words contain the same number of each letter. Return all groups, including singletons, in any order. Empty strings are valid.

Example 1: words = ["abb","bab","ab","","bba"]. Output: [[0,1,4],[2],[3]] in any order. Example 2: words = ["aa","a"]. Output: [[0],[1]]. 0 ≤ n ≤ 100,000; total character count L ≤ 1,000,000.

Constraints: input is immutable; all identifiers and numeric entries are signed 32-bit integers unless specified. Arithmetic uses signed 64-bit integers. Prefer the least expected running-time growth, then avoid unnecessary asymptotic auxiliary storage. Non-adversarial hashing of fixed-size integer keys/tuples has expected amortized constant cost.

options.text: For each word, build a tuple of 26 letter counts and append its index to the map bucket for that tuple. Return the buckets.
options.feedback: The tuple keeps every letter multiplicity, so equality is exactly the requested relation; its length is fixed even when words are long.

options.text: Sort a copied character sequence for each word and use the resulting sorted string as its bucket key.
options.feedback: Sorting characters gives a valid signature, but the fixed alphabet allows direct counts without ordering each word.

options.text: Use the set of distinct letters of a word as its bucket key.
options.feedback: "abb" and "ab" have the same distinct-letter set but different multiplicities.

options.text: Use the sum of character codes as the bucket key.
options.feedback: "ad" and "bc" have equal code sums for consecutive lowercase character codes but different letter counts.

feedback.reason: Use a fixed-alphabet count vector as a complete multiset signature and include the cost of constructing it.
details: For each input word, scan its characters into a fresh 26-counter array, freeze/copy that array into a fixed-size tuple map key, and append the original word index to the key’s bucket. Retain all keys and bucket lists, then copy every bucket’s indices into returned groups.

The 26-counter vector preserves multiplicity: abb differs from ab despite equal distinct-letter sets. Fixed alphabet size makes each signature fixed-sized, but reading arbitrarily long words still costs their total character count.

“For each word, build a tuple of 26 letter counts and append its index to the map bucket for that tuple. Return the buckets.”: The tuple keeps every letter multiplicity, so equality is exactly the requested relation; its length is fixed even when words are long.

“Sort a copied character sequence for each word and use the resulting sorted string as its bucket key.”: Sorting characters gives a valid signature, but the fixed alphabet allows direct counts without ordering each word.
“Use the set of distinct letters of a word as its bucket key.”: "abb" and "ab" have the same distinct-letter set but different multiplicities.
“Use the sum of character codes as the bucket key.”: "ad" and "bc" have equal code sums for consecutive lowercase character codes but different letter counts.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method “Bundle reorderable letter codes — analyzed method”, n is the number of words and L their total number of characters. The alphabet size 26 is a fixed constant; hashing/copying a 26-integer tuple costs constant time. Count increments and list appends have constant/amortized constant cost. Choose its time and auxiliary-space pair. Use the tightest standard bound for the worst legal input for the stated size parameters, with expected time over non-adversarial hashing. Fixed-width integer and fixed-size tuple hash operations take expected amortized O(1); arithmetic, comparison and copying one integer take O(1). Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input and returned result, includes all maps, sets, temporary copies and call stacks. The method is iterative, with constant call-stack space.
constraints: Use the tightest standard bound for the worst legal input for the stated size parameters, with expected time over non-adversarial hashing. Fixed-width integer and fixed-size tuple hash operations take expected amortized O(1); arithmetic, comparison and copying one integer take O(1). Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input and returned result, includes all maps, sets, temporary copies and call stacks. The method is iterative, with constant call-stack space.

options.text: Expected O(L + n + 1) time; O(n + 1) auxiliary space.
Expected O(n + 1) time independent of L; O(n + 1) space.
Expected O(L + n + 1) time; O(1) space.
O(L log(L+1) + n + 1) time; O(L+n+1) space as the tight bound.

feedback.reason: Read all characters and retain signatures plus bucket indices.
details: Use a fixed-alphabet count vector as a complete multiset signature and include the cost of constructing it.
Reading all characters costs O(L); initializing and copying 26 counters per word costs O(n), as do bucket appends and copying the returned indices. Fixed-size tuple hashing gives expected O(L+n+1).
There are at most n keys of 26 integers and exactly n indices in retained bucket lists, plus one temporary 26-counter array. Returned copies are excluded, so O(n+1).
“Expected O(L + n + 1) time; O(n + 1) auxiliary space.”: Correct under the stated expected/amortized hashing model.
“Expected O(n + 1) time independent of L; O(n + 1) space.”: Reading characters to construct signatures costs L in total.
“Expected O(L + n + 1) time; O(1) space.”: The retained bucket lists contain n indices and the map retains its keys.
“O(L log(L+1) + n + 1) time; O(L+n+1) space as the tight bound.”: The fixed method counts a fixed alphabet, without sorting or copying all characters.
